bio: Nargis Khan is a former captain and legendary goalkeeper of the Pakistan women's hockey team, and a member of Pakistan's first women's hockey team. She was born and raised in Lahore, started hockey in 1980 at Lahore College for Women, and played for 17 years before retiring in 1997.

She was given the title of Little Panther by the Ireland team after she conceded only five goals from fifty strikes in the 1983 series, playing in cloth leg guards without a helmet. She received the Lifetime Achievement Award in 2018, has been coaching since 1984, and runs her own women's hockey academy, Roha.

summary: In Episode 14 of Muffled Minds, host Khawar Shahzad sits down with Nargis Khan, the Little Panther of Pakistan hockey, a former captain and legendary goalkeeper of the Pakistan women's hockey team. She started hockey in 1980 at Lahore College for Women, played for Pakistan for 17 years, and gave 45 years of her life to the game, yet she has never received a stipend, match fees or camp allowances.

Nargis tells how she got the title of Little Panther: in the 1983 series against Ireland, playing in cloth leg guards without a helmet, she conceded only five goals from fifty strikes. She talks about the tours that followed, Malaysia, China and Zimbabwe, the Zia era that tried to keep women inside four walls, and the Benazir government that, as a woman prime minister, still did nothing for women's hockey. She also talks about her 1987 trip to England, paid for by teaching tuitions, and about coaching since 1984 and running her own academy, Roha.

The conversation then turns to politics and the state of the game: why she joined PTI in 1996 and stopped supporting it after 2020, the closing of departmental sports, the praise for Maryam Nawaz and the Punjab government, the paper certificate of the 2018 Lifetime Achievement Award, and her proposal for a sports policy that pays players after retirement. It closes with what success means to her, that without financial stability you are not successful, and the Fish Jar question, where she answers that her luck was getting into the Pakistan team and wearing the green colour.

takeaways: Pakistan remembers the medals and forgets the hands that created the history: legends get an award and then nothing.
She played 17 years for Pakistan and never received test match fees or camp daily allowances; the government still owes that money.
Cricket is Pakistan's own child and hockey is the stepchild, although hockey is the national game.
The Zia era held women's hockey back for 11 years, and even a woman prime minister did nothing for it.
She calls the Musharraf era the golden era for women's hockey: teams were sent abroad, cash awards were given and women were supported.
Her 2018 Lifetime Achievement Award was only a piece of paper: each player should have got 10 to 20 lakh with it.
Her sports policy proposal: 10 years of international hockey should mean one crore fifty lakh after retirement.
Success is financial stability: if you are not financially stable, you are not successful.
Her wish: invite foreign women's teams again and restart international hockey as it began in 1983.

teams used to come to Pakistan. Unfortunately, it is a great misfortune. Well, after that, I believe, it was Benazir's government.
